intro: First-week doubts: what a prompt is, where your project lives, what that black window is, and whether any of this will cost you money or break your computer.

preguntas.q: Do I need to know how to code to do this?
preguntas.a: No. Here you don't write code: you hand the job to the AI and learn to check that what it gave you actually works. What you will learn is to explain yourself clearly, put your data in front of it, and catch in time when something's going wrong. It's more like directing a very fast, scatterbrained intern than studying computer science. Start with Lesson 1: in half an hour you understand what ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini really are, and that saves you half the headaches that come later.
preguntas.corta: No. You direct and check; you don't write the code.

preguntas.q: Everyone keeps saying "prompt." What exactly is that?
preguntas.a: A prompt is the text you write to the AI to ask it for something. That's it. It's not a command, there are no magic words, and the person who types the longest doesn't win. What actually changes the result is that the request has five pieces: who you want it to be, what context about you it has, what it has to deliver, what format you want it in, and how you'll know if it's good. With those five, the same request goes from giving you something generic to giving you something you can paste in without rewriting it.
preguntas.corta: The request you write to the AI. That's all it is.

preguntas.q: Is this going to cost me money?
preguntas.a: It depends which door you walk through, and there are two. If you type in the text box of ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, you're through the safe door: you're either on the free version or paying a fixed monthly fee, and when you go over the limit you get throttled, not overcharged. The scary part lives behind the other door, pay-per-use with an API key, which has no cap by default. Entry plans run around $23 a month, but that changes every few months: check the price on the official site before entering a card.
preguntas.corta: With the app, no. With an API key, it can.

preguntas.q: What is an API? I see it everywhere and don't get it.
preguntas.a: An API is the side door through which one program asks another for things without a person clicking buttons. You use ChatGPT by opening the website and typing; your future page would use the API to ask it the same thing at three in the morning while you sleep. That's the practical difference: the API is used when something of yours needs to run on its own. As long as it's you typing and you reading, you don't need it for anything, and you can skip the whole headache.
preguntas.corta: The door two programs use to talk without us.

preguntas.q: And that "key" thing? Is it just a password of mine?
preguntas.a: It's worse than a password. An API key is a long string of letters and numbers, and whoever holds it is you, as far as OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google are concerned: no second question, no code to your phone, no email alerting you. It can burn through your entire balance overnight. That's why it never goes inside code, never gets pasted into a chat, never appears in a screenshot: it goes in a separate file called .env that never leaves your computer. And if it leaks, deleting it from wherever you pasted it doesn't fix anything. You go to the service's website, revoke it, and create a new one, the same day.
preguntas.corta: Worse: it's your username, password, and code, all in one string.

preguntas.q: Where's my project? I've got files scattered everywhere.
preguntas.a: Your project is a folder, and everything it needs has to live inside it. The test is the move: copy that folder onto a USB drive, open it on another computer, and if it works, you have a project; if a lone file got left behind in Downloads, what you had were loose files that vaguely knew each other. The Desktop doesn't count, because it's not a drawer, it's a table: your bank statements sit there next to the fourteen files the AI handed you along the way. Create a folder called projects, lowercase, and put each project in its own subfolder.
preguntas.corta: Your project is a folder. Otherwise, it's just loose files.

preguntas.q: Why does it save as .txt when I named it .md?
preguntas.a: Because Notepad tacks on a .txt at the end on its own when you save. Your file ends up called README.md.txt, and with that added on it stops being what you think it is: no program recognizes it. To avoid this, when saving, change the Type dropdown to All Files and type the full name in quotes if needed. If it's already happened, click the file, press F2, delete the .txt at the end, and say yes when it asks whether you want to change the extension. And if you don't see any .txt at all, it's because you haven't turned on showing file extensions yet.
preguntas.corta: Notepad adds .txt. Remove it with F2.

preguntas.q: I created the .gitignore file and it disappeared. Did it get deleted?
preguntas.a: No, it's right there. What happens is Windows and Mac ship hiding every file whose name starts with a period, and as it happens, two of the most important files in your project start that way: .gitignore and .env.local. You create them, they vanish from view, and you assume they never saved. Go into folder options and turn on showing hidden files, the same way you turn on showing extensions. It's two checkboxes, nothing gets deleted, and you can turn them off again whenever you want.
preguntas.corta: No. Windows and Mac hide files that start with a period.

preguntas.q: Can I leave my project in OneDrive? That's where all my stuff is.
preguntas.a: Better not to. On most Windows machines today, the Desktop and Documents are synced with OneDrive, which means a file can show up in a listing without actually being downloaded; when a program goes to open it, it finds nothing there and throws an error that doesn't mention OneDrive at all. Put it in C:\Users\yourname\projects\ and the problem goes away. And yes, you lose the automatic backup there: that's why you copy the folder by hand on day one, and later on GitHub does it for you, and it also keeps every version, not just the latest.
preguntas.corta: Better not. Take it out of OneDrive and back it up separately.

preguntas.q: My Windows username has an accent mark. Does that cause problems?
preguntas.a: It can, and of the kind you don't see coming. Accent marks, special characters, and spaces in the path (the full address of the folder, written out end to end from the drive down) get handled fine by some tools and choke others, and the error that shows up doesn't mention the accent anywhere. Windows also has an old 260-character limit on that path, and projects nest folders inside folders until they eat through it. The fix is the same for everything: lowercase names, words separated by hyphens, no accents, no special characters, no spaces.
preguntas.corta: It can cause trouble. Use lowercase folder names without accents.

preguntas.q: A huge node_modules folder showed up. Can I delete it?
preguntas.a: You can delete it without worry. It's the folder where pieces of code written by other people, that your project borrows, get downloaded: two or three hundred megabytes and tens of thousands of files you'll never open in your life. You didn't create it, an install command creates it on its own, and that same command recreates it in full. It's the one folder in the project you can delete without any drama. That's exactly why it's always listed in .gitignore, the list of things that never get uploaded anywhere.
preguntas.corta: Borrowed code. Delete it without worry: it comes back on its own.

preguntas.q: What is that black window where you have to type weird stuff?
preguntas.a: It's called a terminal, and it's a window where you give the computer commands by typing them instead of clicking buttons. You type a line, hit Enter, and it answers with text. There's nothing magic or dangerous about it by itself, but two habits save you almost every scare: check which folder you're in before running anything, and never paste a command you don't understand, no matter how convincing whoever handed it to you sounds. One thing worth knowing from the start: what you delete from there doesn't go to the trash bin.
preguntas.corta: The terminal: you give commands by typing instead of clicking.

preguntas.q: I started the project and the window just sits there. Did it freeze?
preguntas.a: No, it's the opposite: it's working. That program is called a development server, and it has to stay running for your project to show up in the browser; that's why it prints a few lines and doesn't give you the cursor back. You stop it with Ctrl+C, both keys at once, inside that same window. And here's what trips everyone up the first day: if you close the window, your page stops showing. Nothing broke, you just switched off the waiter who was serving it.
preguntas.corta: No. It's working. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

preguntas.q: Can this break my computer?
preguntas.a: No. Typing in a chat doesn't touch anything on your machine, and the programs installed for this kind of thing can be uninstalled. The real risk isn't breaking it, it's cluttering it: every installed program eats disk space, updates itself every few weeks, and every so often clashes with something you already had, and the day something fails you won't know which of the six is to blame. That's why here you install as little as possible and only when you need to. The one hard rule for the first few days: never paste a command into the terminal that you don't understand, even if the AI gave it to you.
preguntas.corta: No. The worst that happens is a program fails to start.

preguntas.q: What if I accidentally delete something and lose three days of work?
preguntas.a: It's recoverable, as long as you set up the safety net beforehand. GitHub saves a snapshot of the entire project every time you push changes, so you can go back to yesterday's version, or the one from three weeks ago, in a couple of minutes, and it's all done by dragging files with your mouse, without typing a single command. There's only one thing in all of this with no way back: a key uploaded by mistake. That one can't be un-published, only revoked and replaced.
preguntas.corta: It's recoverable. That's what GitHub is for, with your mouse.

preguntas.q: I told it about my situation yesterday and today it doesn't remember any of it. Is that normal?
preguntas.a: It's normal, and you haven't done anything wrong. The AI doesn't remember: every time you write, the entire conversation gets resent from the start, and whatever no longer fits in that space falls off the edge. That's why a mile-long chat starts getting dumber first, starts skipping rules you set at the beginning, and then forgets entirely. The fix isn't to keep insisting, it's to move: open a new chat and paste in a written handoff of what needs to be known. And save that summary in a file of your own, outside the AI.
preguntas.corta: Yes. It has no memory: it rereads the conversation every time.

preguntas.q: It made something up and said it with total confidence. Can I trust it?
preguntas.a: Trust the shape, not the fact. These tools don't look anything up: they write the most likely continuation, piece by piece, which is why a made-up figure comes out with exactly the same confidence as a true one. Things change when you give it the data yourself, or when the tool actually checks something online, and you can tell because clickable links show up. First-days rule, and don't skip it: names, figures, laws, and prices always get checked against the original source.
preguntas.corta: Not entirely. It writes the most likely thing, not what it knows.

preguntas.q: What do I need to install to start today?
preguntas.a: Today, nothing. The bare minimum to get going is five things and four of them are free accounts: an up-to-date browser is enough for day one. Tutorials start by installing programs because they're written by people who already code and have had everything set up for years; for you that's forty minutes of a wall before you've seen anything of your own on screen, and that's where most people give up. Installing is one of the last things you do, and only once there's a clear sign it's actually needed.
preguntas.corta: Nothing. An up-to-date browser and little else.

preguntas.q: I get a red error I don't understand at all. What do I do?
preguntas.a: Copy it in full and paste it to the AI exactly as it is, without summarizing or rewriting it, with the same attitude you'd have showing an X-ray to a doctor: you don't need to understand it yourself. Two warnings. The real message is almost never where you're looking: it's usually in the terminal, or in the browser console, which opens with F12. And ask for the diagnosis first, not the fix: have it tell you what it thinks is wrong before it touches a single file. That way it doesn't blindly rewrite half your project.
preguntas.corta: Copy it in full and paste it to the AI. Don't summarize.

preguntas.q: Does my course progress get saved?
preguntas.a: Yes, but it's worth knowing where. What you mark as done, your quiz results, and what you write in the notebook stay in your own browser, on that computer. There's no account or server behind it: none of it leaves your machine, which is great for your privacy and a hassle if you switch devices. If you open the course on another computer, or clear your browsing data, you start from zero. Anything you truly want to keep (your prompts, your notes) should also be saved in your project folder.
preguntas.corta: Yes, but only in this browser and on this computer.
